historyReviewBoundary: All 115 histories have author source checks. Final independent review covered metadata and numerical checks for all 115 classes, 12 deeper class targets and source-gap samples in seven classes. It did not independently verify every passage of every cited source.

history.name: Acyclic guanosine-analogue antivirals

starting.description: Antiviral activity of purine analogues anchored the existing program. Elion and Vince recount that Schaeffer's acyclic adenine analogue was observed to be an adenosine-deaminase substrate, suggesting recognition by other enzymes; its observed antiherpes activity led to development of acyclic antivirals. Other accounts describe a different initial inhibitor intention; see conflicts.

inspiration.description: The precursor chemistry modified adenosine, the enzyme's normal substrate; observed enzyme recognition of an acyclic analogue and antiviral activity of related synthetic compounds supplied the aciclovir program's clues.

steps.description: Existing antiviral findings motivated a purine-arabinoside research program, in which diaminopurine arabinoside had measurable antiviral activity.

A substrate observation on an acyclic adenine analogue suggested other enzymes might recognize the non-ring side chain, and an antiviral screen then revealed antiherpes activity and redirected the program toward acyclic analogues.
The guanine analogue aciclovir was unexpectedly much more active than the corresponding diaminopurine analogue.

The existing antiviral aciclovir was adapted into amino-acid esters. A later deliberate oral-prodrug program compared them in rats and selected the L-valyl ester, 256U87, which became valaciclovir; its absorption advantage was not predicted by the first solubility observations.

design.description: Researchers intentionally designed modified adenosine sugar analogues, synthesized and screened purine arabinosides and acyclic nucleoside analogues, compared base substitutions, and investigated selectivity. Later amino-acid esterification of existing aciclovir and comparative animal testing yielded the L-valine prodrug valaciclovir.

circumstances.description: Acyclic analogues were deliberately synthesized and tested, whereas the much greater activity of the guanine analogue was unexpected. Vince describes hypothesis-directed submission of the adenine precursor for antiviral testing, while Biron calls the aciclovir screen random. The later oral-prodrug comparison was planned; the earlier ester group's initial solubility observations did not predict its oral-absorption advantage.

limits: This lineage is anchored in aciclovir and its valaciclovir prodrug. The 1992 prodrug selection was assessed in rats; its urinary-recovery comparison is not a human clinical result.
conflicts: E10/S2 says aciclovir was initially intended as an adenosine-deaminase inhibitor to potentiate vidarabine; E11/S5 names cytosine arabinoside instead. E2/S1 and E9/S4 describe acycloadenosine as a substrate whose observed enzyme recognition suggested antiviral testing. S5 calls the aciclovir screening random, while S4 describes submitting the adenine precursor on the basis of its enzyme-substrate observation. Whether these accounts conflate compounds or distinct intentions is not resolved. Their reported antiviral effects nevertheless supply observation-led starting points.
gaps: The original 1971 Schaeffer et al. enzyme paper is located but its full text was inaccessible; its precise experimental context and the competing initial-intent accounts cannot be resolved from the title.

The 1978 Nature antiviral report was located but not read in full; the 1977 original aciclovir paper and 1992 original rat prodrug report were read in relevant sections, with access details in the receipt.
Vince's presentation was available as an abstract only; no full presentation was read.

humanContributionInterpretation.summary: Inadequate oral aciclovir bioavailability motivated development of a better-absorbed oral prodrug, including valaciclovir.
humanContributionInterpretation.scope: The original antiviral lead was laboratory-based and selection of the valyl ester used rat urinary recovery.
